summary:
CrewPulse is a health monitoring system for astronauts on long-duration missions. NASA’s Human Research Program groups the dangers of human spaceflight into five hazards: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile/closed environments. NASA notes these hazards can feed off one another and worsen effects on the body.

CrewPulse organizes monitoring around those five hazards. It combines wearable-style readings, cabin-environment readings, radiation dose, and short crew check-ins on one dashboard. It compares each astronaut to their own baseline and raises tiered alerts when trends drift. Because medical care and instructions become harder to get from Earth the farther a crew travels, it runs on board without a live connection. It sends compact health summaries to the ground team when a link is available.

Shorter version, if the form has a character limit: “CrewPulse is an offline-capable crew health dashboard built around NASA’s five spaceflight hazards. It tracks each astronaut against a personal baseline, raises tiered alerts, and sends summaries to ground when a link exists.”
details:
What it does

  • Shows each astronaut’s health status grouped by NASA’s five hazards, so a crew member sees why a reading matters.
  • Learns a personal baseline for each astronaut and flags drift from it, rather than only comparing against fixed population limits.
  • Combines several small changes (for example, worse sleep plus lower activity plus a low mood check-in) into one hazard-level status: Normal, Watch, or Alert.
  • Works on board with no Earth connection. When a link is available, it sends a compact summary to a ground-team view.

What it monitors, by hazard

  • Space radiation: cumulative dose and dose-rate spikes, with neutron radiation tracked as its own channel. Related NASA risk: Radiation-Induced Cancers.
  • Isolation and confinement: daily mood and stress check-in, sleep regularity, and a crew-level teamwork check. Related NASA risks: Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders, Inadequate Teamwork, Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules.
  • Distance from Earth: this is a design driver rather than a measured signal. It shapes the offline-first architecture, on-board decision support, and store-and-forward summaries.
  • Gravity fields: exercise logs, resting heart-rate trend, and a short balance/coordination self-check after gravity transitions. Related NASA risks: Cardiovascular Adaptations, Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness, Altered Sensorimotor and Vestibular Function, Spaceflight-Induced Bone Changes.
  • Hostile/closed environments: cabin temperature, pressure, lighting, noise, and a symptom log. A blood-oxygen reading covers hypoxia. Related NASA risks: Hypoxia, Altered Immune System Responses, Host-Microorganism Interactions.

How it works

  1. Data input: a simulated data generator stands in for wearables, cabin sensors, and a dosimeter. The data format is organized as a consistent set of physiological and psychological measures, in the spirit of NASA’s Standard Measures study.
  2. Baseline: the first days of data set each astronaut’s normal range. A rolling baseline then detects deviations.
  3. Rules and trends: simple, explainable rules combine signals into a status for each hazard.
  4. Alerts: three tiers (Normal, Watch, Alert). Every alert shows which signals triggered it and which NASA-listed risk it relates to.
  5. Views: a crew view (the astronaut sees their own data first) and a ground-team view that receives summaries when a link is available.

Tools used React 18 (hooks); htm (JSX-style templates); Chart.js 4 for charts; HTML5, CSS3 (CSS variables, glassmorphism, animations); JavaScript (ES6); inline SVG ring gauges and sparklines; a JavaScript data simulator for crew vitals, cabin readings, and cumulative dose; NASA DONKI API (solar flares); "Inter and JetBrains Mono fonts" jsDelivr CDN; GitHub Pages for hosting; OBS Studio and CapCut for the demo video. Chart.js, GitHub for hosting.

Goals

  • Make hazard-based health monitoring visible on one screen.
  • Catch drift early, before a small change becomes a mission problem.
  • Keep working when contact with Earth is delayed or unavailable.
  • Provide a foundation that real sensors could plug into later.

Limitations (be upfront about these)

  • This is a hackathon prototype using simulated data.
  • Thresholds are illustrative, not clinically validated.
  • It is decision support for a crew and flight surgeon, not a diagnostic or medical device.

Use of SI or NASA Data

CrewPulse uses NASA Human Research Program (HRP) and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) resources as the basis for its design. It does not use real astronaut health data.

NASA HRP: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight. The five hazards are the dashboard’s top-level structure. NASA’s point that the hazards can compound one another is why CrewPulse combines signals instead of tracking each in isolation. NASA’s note that Mars is about 140 million miles away, with a trip of roughly three years, drove the offline-first design. NASA names self-sufficiency as key for deep space missions.

NASA HRP: Risks of Human Spaceflight. We mapped specific NASA-listed risks to monitored signals: sleep and schedules, behavioral conditions, teamwork, fitness, cardiovascular adaptation, immune response, hypoxia, and radiation-induced cancers. Alert messages name the related risk.

The dashboard also pulls recent solar-flare events from NASA’s DONKI space-weather database (api.nasa.gov) and displays them as context for the radiation hazard. Crew vitals and dose values remain simulated.

NASA HRP: Ongoing Research.

  • ARCHeR monitored astronauts’ well-being, activity, and sleep on Artemis II. It inspired our sleep, activity, and well-being signals.
  • Standard Measures collects a consistent set of physiological and psychological measurements. It inspired our common data format.
  • Tempus Pro tested a telemedicine device that integrates health data for possible remote, near real-time diagnoses. It inspired our combined data view and the ground-team view.

CSA: Monitoring Radiation for Astronaut Health. The article describes the Canadian Active Neutron Spectrometer (CANS), a compact, autonomous instrument for measuring neutron radiation in space. It notes neutrons contribute about 30% of total radiation on the ISS. This led us to track neutron dose as a separate channel and to design the radiation module around continuous, autonomous measurement.

CSA: Why Do We Conduct Science Experiments in Space? It lists the added risks of Moon and Mars missions: more weightlessness, more radiation exposure, longer isolation, communication delays, and less ability to rely on Earth. We used this list as our requirements checklist.

Transparency: all sensor values in the demo are simulated, and the thresholds are illustrative.

Next Steps:

  • Real wearable and dosimeter inputs.
  • Validation with flight surgeons.
  • Space-weather-triggered radiation alerts.
  • A real neutron-dose channel.

References

  • NASA, 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight: https://www.nasa.gov/hrp/hazards/
  • NASA, Risks of Human Spaceflight: https://www.nasa.gov/hrp/risks/
  • NASA, Ongoing HRP Research in Space: https://www.nasa.gov/hrp/ongoing-hrp-research/
  • CSA, Monitoring Radiation for Astronaut Health: https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/news/articles/2026/2026-02-26-monitoring-radiation-astronaut-health.asp
  • CSA, Why Do We Conduct Science Experiments in Space?: https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/iss/science/why-do-we-conduct-science-experiments-in-space.asp
